  "text": "The station clock had stopped at eleven seventeen, though the trains still came through twice an hour.

Martin found his father beneath it, holding a paper bag against his chest.

“You could have waited inside.”

“Too warm.”

It was November. His father’s ears were red.

They crossed the car park without speaking. At the passenger door, his father paused to look back at the clock.

“Your mother would have written to someone.”

“She did. Years ago.”

“Did she?”

Martin unlocked the car.

The bag contained six tulip bulbs and a receipt. His father settled it between his shoes.

“I thought we’d put them by the kitchen window.”

Martin started the engine, then switched it off. Across the road, a woman was trying to close a pushchair one-handed.

“The flat hasn’t got a garden, Dad.”

“I know that.”

“We could get a pot.”

His father bent to straighten the top of the bag, folding it twice along the same crease.

“Your place, I meant.”

“Oh.”

A train passed behind the station wall. They felt it briefly through the seats.

“I’ve still got her trowel,” Martin said.

“Well, you’ll need it.”

At home, the soil beneath the kitchen window was hard. His father watched from the doorstep while Martin fetched a fork instead.

“Not so close together.”

Martin moved the first bulb.

“Like that?”

His father came down the step and crouched beside him. He took off one glove and pressed his fingers into the earth.

“Another inch.”

When they finished, Martin brought out two mugs. His father stayed by the window, holding his with both hands.

“You’ll see them from the sink,” he said."
